summary:
Verdict: NEW for a real EmberGen-style volumetric fire, smoke or explosion simulation. It has never been built, never attempted, and never removed. The only things that exist are simple sprite effects, a design direction, and systems that track disasters without drawing them.

Evidence, in the four categories:

(1) EXISTS, but basic and never used in the world. The particle system went in with v0.90.0 (commit b72a00c8, 2026-04-07). Particles are flat camera-facing dots, not volumes. data/particles.ron defines 15 emitter types, including "fire" (line 9), "smoke" (26), "sparks" (43), "explosion" (181), "welding" and "engine_exhaust". The explosion is 300 glowing dots with a lifetime of 0.3 to 1.0 s. The simulation moved to the GPU in v0.1068.0 (146c3335) and became the default in v0.1085.0 (dabed6a2). Neither step added density, temperature, smoke shading or fluid behaviour.

The world only ever creates four emitter types: leaf_drift (src/lib.rs:3839), dive_bubbles (3860), space_dust (3921) and rain/snow (4140). Fire, smoke, sparks and explosion appear only in a doc-comment example (src/renderer/particles.rs:8). No in-game code ever creates them.

(2) DESIGNED, not built.
- The realistic-first rule of 2026-08-02 names "EmberGen-class volumetric effects" as a target (CLAUDE.md:836; docs/history/journal-archive-2026-08.md, the 2026-08-02 entry).
- The overnight arc of 2026-08-03 was told to "learn from SpeedTree + EmberGen". What it actually shipped was tree work only.
- The one written technical direction for smoke is in commit 24e8e3ce (2026-08-26), now archived at docs/history/priorities-archive-2026-08-to-09.md:3347-3352. It says the 2030 version of a smoke grenade "is a small dense voxel grid marched against the SAME scattering model", and that we should "feed a local volume into the cloud march rather than building a second billboard system".
- docs/design/voxel-terrain.md:7-12 quotes the operator (2026-07-26) asking for asteroid craters, explosions, shockwave, smoke cloud and debris. Line 3 says "Nothing here is built yet". Rung 6 (lines 82-84) is the impact-crater step, and it plans to reuse "the existing particles/audio".
- docs/design/weather-water-roadmap.md:85-104 sketches a meteor storm and a fire storm, with smoke columns running through the cloud system.

(3) Simulation without visuals.
- src/systems/disasters.rs has MeteorImpact and AsteroidImpact (lines 36-37, 104-105). Each carries a vfx_id string ("vfx_meteor", "vfx_asteroid"), but nothing outside that file reads it. The system is not registered (tests/engine_wiring_lint.rs:41). docs/PRIORITIES.md:63-66 says so directly: "nothing outside that file reads them, so a wildfire is invisible."
- src/systems/fire.rs (fuel, spread, suppression, lines 1-9) with data/fire_system.ron is an unregistered scaffold (tests/engine_wiring_lint.rs:71).
- src/systems/atmosphere.rs:473-477 does run. When a sealed room has a flammable atmosphere and an ignition source, it logs "EXPLOSION" and applies damage. Nothing is drawn.
- The oxygen-driven fire and smoke spread design is in docs/design/engine-architecture.md:702-710. It is text only.

(4) What the operator is probably remembering. Most likely several real things blended together:
- JangaFX is listed as a partner organization on his old Project Universe site (docs/history/project-universe-site/pages/organizations.txt, archived 2023-07-10). That fits "forever ago".
- The v0.90.0 release notes (April 2026) listed "fire, smoke, explosion" emitters.
- EmberGen was named as a target on 2026-08-02/03.
- The volumetric cloud renderer is the one EmberGen-style technique that actually shipped: a ray-marched scattering volume (src/renderer/clouds.rs, assets/shaders/pbr/40-clouds.wgsl, 41-cloud-bodies.wgsl, 45-cloud-temporal.wgsl).

`git log --all -i --grep=embergen` returns nothing. No commit ever claimed to build EmberGen-style functionality.

The real gap: build a small local density and temperature grid (fire, smoke, soot) that feeds the existing cloud ray-march and its scattering model, with flame colour driven by temperature. Then wire it to the existing fire, disaster and atmosphere systems. That one mechanism would serve both the fire props and the asteroid impact. The doc direction already exists for it, so extend that rather than adding a second billboard system. There are also no 3D models of fire props: assets/models/ holds only furniture, plants and a beam .blend. The fire staff exists only as a written guide (data/library/fire_staff_materials.md).

summary:
No EmberGen-class volumetric fire or explosion code exists anywhere in the repo: there is no GPU fluid grid and no combustion model. EmberGen appears only as a stated goal: CLAUDE.md:836 (the realistic-first norm, commit c71bc90b, 2026-08-01) and two August 2026 journal entries (docs/history/journal-archive-2026-08.md lines 14 and 98).

The operator's memory is probably the "fire", "smoke", "sparks" and "explosion" entries in data/particles.ron, added in v0.90.0 (b72a00c8, 2026-04-07). They are simple sprite recipes: flat camera-facing dots whose colour and size change in a straight line over their lifetime. The particle system was not drawn on screen until v0.966 (96d5b69f, 2026-07-25), and no code has ever spawned fire, smoke, explosion, welding, engine_exhaust, healing, magic_sparkle or bubbles.

What is live today is weather and ambience only:
- rain and snow, on the CPU plus a GPU compute pool
- leaves drifting among trees
- bubbles while diving
- dust in space while flying
- "dust" during a tornado weather event and "sparks" during a meteor-shower event

Fire and disasters are simulation scaffolds with no visual output. They are not registered, so they never run. The disaster system names effects like "vfx_asteroid" and "vfx_meteor", but nothing reads those names. The fire system only burns down abstract fuel numbers. Wildfire exists only as a data row that nothing draws.

The glow (bloom) pass is built but never called. The frame renders straight into an 8-bit screen buffer, and only the main 3D surface shader applies tone mapping. Bright particles therefore clip to flat white-yellow.

Also missing: heat haze, particles that fade softly where they touch geometry, sprite textures or animated frames, flame trails, smoke that reacts to sunlight, shadows from local lights, and craters created at runtime.

Parts that could be reused for real fire:
- a working compute-shader path (src/renderer/particles_gpu.rs)
- 3D textures and a full volumetric ray-march with frame-to-frame accumulation (the cloud system, but built for planet scale and driven by noise, not simulation)
- a tiled light system that takes up to 2048 point, spot or line lights per frame
- a glowing lava material (shader type 11)
- tsunami and rogue-wave shapes on the ocean surface, triggered only by a developer command

exists.what: CPU particle simulation and emitter management. Each emitter is a point or a jittered box volume; spawning is a random cone with a speed range; motion is constant acceleration (gravity) only; colour and size change in a straight line from start to end; the spawn rate is capped at what the pool can sustain. Measured cost is 17-20 ns per particle per frame; rayon is used above 50k particles. The module doc calls it a 'GPU particle system' but the simulation runs on the CPU.

gaps: The prop itself: an emitter carries only a position, with no parent transform (src/renderer/particles.rs:163-186). A wick would be driven the way leaf_drift is, by rewriting e.position every frame (src/lib.rs:3830-3842). No held-item or first-person model renderer and no skeletal animation were found, so nothing yet supplies a moving wick transform.

Trail persistence: particles already live independently of their emitter and are shifted with the floating origin (particles.rs:480-487), so a moving emitter does leave a trail. But every particle spawned in a frame appears at the single current position (spawn_particle, particles.rs:330-335). At poi and staff tip speeds of about 10-20 m/s and 60 fps that means 17-33 cm gaps between clumps. Needed: spawn positions spread along the previous-to-current path (ideally the swept arc) and inherited emitter velocity; neither exists.

Motion model: constant acceleration only (particles.rs:239-241, 255-256; particle_sim.wgsl:139-140). There is no drag toward the surrounding air, no buoyancy from temperature, no per-particle wind, no turbulence or curl noise and no collision. Believable flame tongues and smoke need drag, temperature buoyancy and curl noise.

Look: the sprite is a procedural soft disc (particles.wgsl:76-95). The pipeline binds only the camera and a frame uniform (particles.rs:570-586), so there are no texture or animated-frame slots and no rotation. Colour and size are two-point straight-line changes (particles.rs:359-367). Fire needs a temperature-to-colour (blackbody) ramp; smoke needs density-based shading.
Smoke lighting: particles receive only one day/night brightness number (particles.wgsl:19-27, 92). No sun direction, shadowing, self-shadowing or scattering model, so smoke cannot look lit.

No soft fade where particles meet geometry (the particle pass never samples depth) and no back-to-front sorting (emitters are concatenated in order, particles.rs:495-508). Smoke quads will show hard lines against the prop, body and ground, and will pop when order changes.

Brightness and glow: there is no high-range render target and bloom is never applied (bloom.rs:169 apply is unused). Particles write rgb*(1+emissive) straight into 8-bit sRGB with no tone mapping, while 3D surfaces use per-fragment ACES (80-fragment-shared.wgsl:436-442). Flames clip to flat yellow-white with no glare. Needed: a floating-point scene target, one shared tone-mapping pass, and bloom wired in.

Firelight: particles emit no light. A flame needs a per-frame light (a line light along the wick, light.rs:111-113) added in the light gather at lib.rs:14631, with data-driven flicker. light_types.ron has no flame or flicker type, and no local-light shadow code exists, so neither the performer nor the prop will cast firelight shadows.
Heat haze: there is no distortion or refraction pass and no copy of the rendered scene. Needed: render to an offscreen target first, then offset screen UVs by a heat mask.

The GPU pool handles one emitter, respawns dead slots at the current origin, and draws alpha only (particles_gpu.rs:26-30; overlay_draw.rs:323). GPU flames would need an emitter table, a dead-slot list with atomics for bursts and trails, and an additive/emissive draw.

EmberGen-class fire (the realistic-first route) does not exist in any form: no 3D fluid grid, advection, pressure solve, vorticity or combustion step (fuel + O2 -> heat + smoke + CO2/H2O). Parts that do exist: compute pipelines proven on a real device (particles_gpu.rs:345-391), 3D textures (cloud_noise.rs), and a volumetric ray-march with frame-to-frame accumulation (40-clouds.wgsl:4758, cloud_resolve.rs). A spinning prop's flame would need a simulation box that travels with the wick, or sparse bricks. The affordable shape is probably a hybrid: GPU particles or a ribbon for the flame at the wick, plus a coarse grid for smoke.

Combustion chemistry is not connected. FireSystem does not consume O2 or add CO2, CO, water vapour or soot to the room gas tracking in atmosphere.rs. The chemistry data has kerosene, CO2 and CO rows but no heat of combustion, flame temperature, soot yield or flash point columns (data/chemistry/compounds.csv header). The fields in fire_system.ron are never read.

Asteroid impact has no visuals at all. DisasterSystem is unregistered and its vfx_id is never read. The 'explosion' emitter is 300 sprites at 3-8 m/s, firecracker scale (particles.ron:181-197). Also missing: a fireball volume, a shock ring, a pressure wave, ejecta or debris physics (the rapier wrapper in src/physics/mod.rs is unused for this), runtime craters, a sound delay by distance, and the explosion.ogg file. The ocean tsunami field is the only impact-related visual that exists.

The docs overstate or misstate the particle system:
- docs/FEATURES.md:1334-1338 and 2402-2404, and docs/STATUS.md:333, claim 12 emitters including steam, ember and lightning, and point at particle.wgsl. There are actually 15 definitions, with no steam, ember or lightning, and the live shader is particles.wgsl.
- data/particles.ron:2 and particles.rs:4 claim hot reload, but the file is loaded once at boot (lib.rs:1699), and the particle shader is compiled in with include_str! (particles.rs:568), outside the shader hot-reload.
- docs/contributor/ENGINE_REFERENCE.md:409 still lists the particle system as unbuilt.
- particles.rs:1 calls itself a GPU particle system, but the simulation runs on the CPU.
Any new flame shape has to go into assets/shaders/particles.wgsl. The v0.1065 snowflake (da795adc) was written into the unused particle.wgsl, so the shape field has never reached the screen.

Possible double rain (not checked at runtime, because this task forbade booting the game). The comment at src/lib.rs:4036-4042 says the CPU rain and snow emitters stay inactive when gpu_particles is on. The list at lib.rs:4108-4109 still switches them on, so both the CPU and GPU pools appear to run and draw.
The meteor_shower weather event only turns on the 'sparks' emitter 13 m above the camera, with gravity -9.8 (lib.rs:4029, 4126-4150). It looks like a spark fountain overhead, not meteors.

Cost reference points: the CPU path costs 17-20 ns per particle per frame (particles.rs:233-234) and goes parallel above 50k (223). The GPU pool uses 84 bytes per slot, and a 128 MiB buffer holds 4.19M particles (particles_gpu.rs:22-24). Particles get 5% of the frame (budget_systems.ron:124). For a single fire prop, the GPU cost will come from large overlapping quads near the camera, not particle count. An EmberGen-class approach would be dominated by the grid simulation and ray-march; the planet cloud march only became affordable with frame-to-frame accumulation.

summary:
The game can load 3D models, but they only work for machines, furniture and plants. Items and anything held in the hands have no models at all. There are no flow-arts props in the game data. The one real asset is a sourced Library guide on building a fire staff.

**How models load.** One glTF loader in src/assets/mod.rs does all of it: `decode_first_primitive` at 261-297, the textured variant at 320-390 and the cached `load_gltf` at 399-432, using `gltf = "1.4"` (Cargo.toml:44). It reads only the FIRST mesh's FIRST primitive and ignores node transforms. It decodes only the base-colour texture, so the normal and roughness maps that ship with the photoscans are never used. The vertex type (src/renderer/mesh.rs:9-13) holds only position, normal and UV, with no tangents, bone joints/weights or vertex colours.

**Which objects can have a model:**
- A machine or furniture row can declare `model: Some(path)` in data/machines/home.ron (field defined at src/machines.rs:116-123). This shipped in v0.734 (c9163b42), and textured models followed in v0.993 (68e09967).
- Models are scaled to the height declared in `size` (v0.1324, 3bafa7c8 and b1aa6f34).
- Decorations, crop growth-stage models and tree species are also data-driven.
- Procedural geometry exists: primitive builders (mesh.rs:171-685, including tube and polytube) and a large spline-lofted tree and plant generator (tree_mesh.rs, 6354 lines; plant_mesh.rs, 895 lines).
- Since 9f7910e9 (2026-09-19) the release zip includes assets/models (188 MB) and assets/textures (build-desktop.yml:90-111, 284-291).

**Items have no model link.** Neither data/items.csv (columns at line 16) nor `ItemDef` (src/systems/inventory/mod.rs:277-295) has a model field. data/equipment.csv adds damage and reach numbers for items worn in the single "hands" slot (data/inventory/equipment_slots.json). The F-key melee swing reads those numbers (src/lib.rs:11865-11907) but nothing appears on screen.

**No held items, player body or animation:**
- First person has no hands or held item.
- Third person orbits an empty point (src/renderer/camera.rs:1147-1180); no mesh for the local player was found.
- Remote players and NPCs are a box plus a sphere (src/lib.rs:9044-9099). The avatar on the character-select podium is built from boxes (src/engine/world_load.rs:14-63).
- There is no skeletal animation and no glTF animation import (docs/PRIORITIES.md:1083, docs/design/multi-agent-workflow.md:108-117). The only object animation is rigid door panels (src/systems/door_anim.rs).
- The Rapier joint sets exist (src/physics/mod.rs:19-20), but nothing creates a joint, so there is no rope or chain simulation for poi or meteors.

**Flow-arts items: none.** No staff for spinning, poi, fire axe, darts or meteors, fans, hoops, wick, dip can, fire-blanket item, or naphtha / white-gas / lamp-oil fuel item. Nearest existing items:
- `staff_0`, an oak blunt weapon (items.csv:107, crafted by recipes.csv:88)
- `torch_handheld_0` (items.csv:466), `lantern_oil_0` (467), `candle_0` (464), `campfire_kit_0` (494)
- `fire_extinguisher_0` (346), `fuel_refined_0` (228), `rope_0` (235)
- `chain` and `bearing` components (components.csv:20 and 18)

The fire blanket exists only as a suppression-system row (data/fire_system.ron:258-276).

**The fire staff guide.** data/library/fire_staff_materials.md (664 lines, a copy of docs/user/making/fire_staff_materials.md; commits 972582da, 113e4395, 1a6382f3, 2773ef75) is sourced from NASA, NIOSH, CAMEO and DuPont data. It covers:
- shaft alloys
- wick blends
- heat breaks
- a fuel table with flash points, burn times, soot and radiant heat (lines 340-356)

summary: No combustion simulation runs in the game today. A small fire ticker exists (src/systems/fire.rs, added in v0.142.0, commit 5ffea893, 2026-05-01), but it is never registered. The system list at src/lib.rs:1055-1327 has no FireSystem, HvacSystem, MedicalSystem or DisasterSystem. No code anywhere attaches the Fire, Flammable or FireSuppressor components (the only `Fire {` literal is fire.rs:78). Even if it were switched on, its model is a unitless 0-1 `intensity` plus `fuel_remaining` seconds. It burns 1 unit of fuel per second at full intensity (fire.rs:21, 117), spreads by a random roll within `ignition_dist` (fire.rs:130-137) and takes a flat 1 HP/s from anything within 1.5 m (fire.rs:25-27, 139-145). It has no fuel type, temperature, oxygen, smoke, gas output, light or burns. Its data file, data/fire_system.ron, has 8 fire behaviours, 8 suppression systems and 10 damage effects with temperatures and smoke factors. It is parsed into untyped `Vec<ron::Value>` (fire.rs:31-36) and tick() never reads it. The status IDs it names (debuff_smoke_inhalation, debuff_burn_minor/severe, debuff_poisoned, debuff_poor_visibility, debuff_low_oxygen; fire_system.ron:335-399) do not exist in data/status_effects.csv. The only live gas simulation is AtmosphereSystem (registered at lib.rs:1070, made live in v0.617, commit 310714e4). It holds one 14,000 m3 home air volume (engine/home_spawn.rs:36) as a gas-percent map. Three occupants use O2 and add CO2, and powered scrubbers offset them (atmosphere.rs:407-429). Its explosive-limit and toxic-threshold tables are hardcoded match arms (atmosphere.rs:195-237) that duplicate data/chemistry/gases.csv. Its code that hurts entities for toxic gas or explosions (atmosphere.rs:431-486) needs an `InEnclosedSpace` component that nothing attaches, and nothing spawns the `IgnitionSource` marker (atmosphere.rs:151). So the only thing that reaches the player is the O2-only `breathable` flag. It passes from AirStatus to EnvironmentContext.oxygenated (lib.rs:5741-5758) and then to the blood-oxygen drain in FoodSystem. The player does have more than a health bar. The Vitals component tracks satiation, hydration, energy, oxygen, body_temp_c and waste (ecs/components.rs:79-110). Live health drains are starvation, dehydration, suffocation, freezing, heat exhaustion, high g and status-effect damage over time (food.rs:476-630), and there is a death-cause line. The in-world HUD, however, shows only a health bar (gui/pages/hud.rs:101-118). The other meters, body temperature, a sealed/EXPOSED line and effect chips appear only on the Inventory page (gui/pages/inventory.rs:1431-1520). Several pieces would work the moment something triggers them: status rows `burning` (8 damage every 2 s), `poisoned`, `toxic_atmosphere` and `overheated` (status_effects.csv:46, 47, 80, 54) would be applied by the live effect tick (food.rs:601-626), but nothing applies them. Burn-degree conditions 1-3 exist in data/medical.ron:105-139, but MedicalSystem is dormant. The fire, smoke and sparks particle emitters are defined in data/particles.ron:9-58, but nothing spawns them (spawn call sites are only leaf_drift, dive_bubbles, space_dust and precipitation, lib.rs:3839-4140). Infinite-of-X violations: the explosive-limit and toxic-threshold tables are hardcoded match arms (atmosphere.rs:195-237) instead of reading data/chemistry/gases.csv, which already has explosive_range_percent_low/high and auto_ignition_temp_k. FireSystem's rates are hardcoded constants (fire.rs:20-27) instead of fire_behaviors.

No visual or audio hookup: the fire, smoke and sparks particle defs are never spawned. No fire entity gives off a point light, although the light list supports 256 to 2048 lights (lib.rs:14676). No flame colour or brightness comes from soot. Held light items (torch_handheld_0, lantern_oil_0, candle_0) give no light. Nothing exists for volumetric flame or smoke.

UI can't show a fire hazard at a glance: the HUD is a single health bar (hud.rs:101-118). Vitals, body temperature and effects appear only on the Inventory page, with no in-world warning for oxygen, smoke, heat or burns. Nothing displays air quality beyond O2/CO2 (no CO, particulates or visibility).

No flow-arts props anywhere in items.csv, recipes or models (fire staff, contact staff, poi, fire axe, fire darts or meteors, fans, hoops), and no safety kit such as a fire blanket as a usable item wired to suppression (fire_blanket exists only as a fire_system.ron suppression entry).

Asteroid impact (secondary): AsteroidImpact is a 50 km, 30 s, 500 damage-per-second Force area that chains to earthquake and tsunami (disasters.rs:105, 124). It has no heat pulse, fireball, air blast or shockwave travel time, ejecta, crater or ignition of flammables. DisasterSystem is unregistered and its vfx_id is read by nothing.
notes: docs/design/gameplay-loop-map.md:235-247 calls FireSystem, MedicalSystem and DisasterSystem 'Dormant but complete'. For FireSystem that overstates it: the code runs, but it ignores its own data file, oxygen, temperature and products. The same doc (lines 240-247) puts fire, disease and disasters as the LAST rung of the risk-layer closure ladder, as homestead threats that the habitat systems defend against.

The quickest real carrier for a lit prop is to reuse what is live rather than revive fire.rs as it stands. That means: a fuel data table built from the Library guide's sourced numbers; a per-wick component (fuel mass, burn rate, soot factor) ticked by a registered system; each wick adding a moving point light and spawning the existing fire, smoke and sparks emitters; combustion products written into the existing AtmosphereSystem composition map; a toxicity or CO field added to EnvironmentContext so the FoodSystem vitals pass can apply the existing toxic_atmosphere, poisoned, burning and overheated rows; and heat exposure mapped to the medical.ron burn degrees once MedicalSystem is registered.

The live status-effect tick (food.rs:601-626) already turns damage_per_tick and tick_interval_s into per-second drains and records the death cause. Any new condition row (for example smoke_inhalation or carbon_monoxide) needs only a CSV row plus one effects.apply() call; no new tick code is required.
src/reactions.rs and data/reactions.json are the chat emoji reaction palette, not chemical reactions. Don't confuse them with combustion.

When fire content is authored, docs/user/making/fire_staff_materials.md is the sourced, dated reference to seed data from (flash-point ranges from NIOSH and CAMEO; burn times explicitly labelled community figures; soot drives radiant heat). Per CLAUDE.md, carry those source labels into the data rather than restating figures from memory, and give the toxic-gas thresholds in atmosphere.rs (CO 50 ppm and so on) the same sourced treatment.

summary:
I compared the repo's chemistry data (C:/Humanity/data/chemistry/alloys.csv, elements.csv, compounds.csv, gases.csv and toxins.csv) and the two Library guides (C:/Humanity/docs/user/making/metals_and_alloys.md and fire_staff_materials.md) against the 2026-09-24 research files. "R/" below means docs/reference/research/2026-09-24-fire-performance/. I found 54 conflicts, listed in gaps[] as C1-C54, each with both values and what each rests on. Nothing was resolved and nothing was edited. Where two research files disagree with each other, the entry says which one the repo matches; alloy-corrections.json is the audit layer over aluminium.json, titanium.json and steels-others.json.

The five that matter most:
1. **Melting points in alloys.csv use two different bases.** 7075 and 2024 carry the liquidus (908 K and 911 K), while 6061 carries the solidus (855 K). The research gives the 7075 solidus as 477 C and the 2024 solidus as 502 C.
2. **The fire staff guide's "starts to fail" table uses melting points.** The research puts the permanent strength loss of T6 aluminium at roughly 150-260 C, and the service ceiling of Ti-6Al-4V at about 325-400 C.
3. **Fuel flash points in the fire guide conflict with manufacturers' safety data sheets.** Examples: camp fuel is grouped with VM&P naphtha, lamp oil is placed inside the kerosene range when it is actually 83.5-121 C, kerosene's lower bound is given as 35 C against the ASTM D3699 minimum of 38 C, and denatured alcohol is given as 11-13 C against 7 C on the product sheet.
4. **The guide's titanium claims conflict with the research.** It says titanium shafts are nearly absent from the market and titanium is the lowest-conductivity metal. The research found Fusion Arts titanium staffs, widely stocked Grade 9 CWSR tube, and CP titanium at 22 W/m-K, above stainless at 14.6-16.3.
5. **compounds.csv marks teflon, zinc oxide, titanium dioxide and kerosene as non-toxic.** The research documents fume or aspiration hazards for each.

The repo files were last changed in these commits: alloys.csv 6845aa5f, compounds.csv db1e98e8, elements.csv b8c1c6db, metals guide 459c74ae, fire guide 2773ef75.

Element table, used for Al, Ti, Zn, Cd, Pb and Mg melting point, boiling point, density and conductivity

Compounds. The only fuel or fume rows are kerosene (line 142), methanol (48), ethanol (47), isopropanol (49), propane and butane (40-41), octane (42), benzene (43), teflon (101), zinc_oxide (114), titanium_dioxide (8) and magnesium_oxide (167). There is no flash_point column.
Gases: CO (line 8), HCl (34), phosgene (26), formaldehyde (39). No fuel-vapour rows, and nothing that conflicts with the research.
Toxins: cadmium (57), chromium_vi (61), benzene (55), methanol (72), lead (37, 68). No rows for metal-fume fever, polymer-fume fever, n-hexane or hydrocarbon aspiration.
Metals and Alloys Library guide, sourced from NASA, DOE, Army and OSHA. It was written 25 minutes before the alloys.csv rewrite, so its data-file section is stale.
Fire Staff Materials Library guide, covering shaft, wick, shield, grip, hardware, fuel, sizing and cost

Research files dated 2026-09-24: aluminium, titanium, steels-others, alloy-corrections (79 audit entries over the three alloy files), fuel-identities, fuel-use, heated-fumes. length-sizing and wall-thickness were out of scope.

Ti-6Al-4V is used annealed up to about 400 C (Fine Tubes), with creep resistance to 325 C (TIMET) [R/titanium.json:284]. summary:
EmberGen-class volumetric fire was never built. The repo only names EmberGen as a "north star" for future work (C:/Humanity/CLAUDE.md:836; C:/Humanity/docs/history/journal-archive-2026-08.md:14 and :98), and `git log --grep=embergen` returns nothing.

What does exist for fire:
- **A generic particle system.** It draws camera-facing sprites, with a CPU path and a GPU pool that holds one emitter at a time and was built for rain and snow. Its fire, smoke, sparks, explosion and welding definitions exist, but no code ever spawns them.
- **A fire system with no visuals.** It tracks fuel, spread and damage only.
- **An AsteroidImpact disaster** whose effect id, "vfx_asteroid", nothing reads.
- **A low-range 8-bit colour target.** The scene renders into an 8-bit sRGB target, each material converts its own brightness to display range, and bloom is built but switched off. Any flame brighter than white gets clipped.

**What a 2030-grade engine would do for dozens of fire props in an MMO: three tiers.**
- **Tier A, every prop at any distance.** Treat the flame as a trail of burning gas left behind in the air. Emit small "flame parcels" continuously along the path the wick travelled during the frame, not in bursts at its end-of-frame position. Colour each parcel from its temperature using the real blackbody colour curve (a precomputed table). Add soot that absorbs light and the thin blue CH*/C2* band at the base. Give each wick one light whose brightness is set from real light output in lumens and which flickers.
- **Tier B, the nearest 1 to 4 flames.** Run a live GPU fire simulation on a grid anchored in the world around the performer, which stores only the cells that contain fire. NVIDIA Flow is the open reference: it has a combustion model and is BSD-3 licensed since PhysX 5.6 / Flow 2.2. Its airflow pushes the Tier A parcels around.
- **Tier C, one-off effects such as explosions and impacts.** This is what EmberGen actually is: a GPU fluid solver used to author effects ahead of time, not code that runs inside the game. Its output is baked into animated texture sheets (with motion vectors, emissive and six-way lighting maps), or into OpenVDB volume sequences. The in-game renderer ray-marches those volumes with the machinery the Nubis-style clouds already use.

All three tiers assume the planned move to a 16-bit linear HDR colour buffer.

**The single most convincing cue for poi and staffs (finding #1):** the flame is a trail of burning vapour left in the air, not a sprite stuck to the wick. The current code spawns a whole frame's particles at the wick's end-of-frame position. At about 10 m/s and 60 fps that breaks a trail into clumps 16.7 cm apart. The biggest cue at mid range (finding #2) is the warm flickering light sweeping over the ground.

Numbers marked as derived estimates must be measured before they go into data. The test rig cannot yet place a burning prop, so a showcase setting for that is a prerequisite for every acceptance test below.

gaps: #1 THE FLAME IS A TRAIL LEFT IN THE AIR, NOT A SPRITE ON THE WICK (0.5-30 m; medium cost, the top cue for poi and staffs). MISSING CUE: a moving fire prop reads fake when its flame is glued to the wick, either standing upright or breaking into a string of blobs. Real flames lie as a continuous tapering tongue along the wick's recent path. REAL BEHAVIOUR: fuel vapour leaves the wick and burns where it was released. A staff tip or poi head at about 2 rev/s on a 0.7-0.8 m radius moves at about 9-13 m/s (derived estimate). That swamps the flame's buoyant rise of about 1-2 m/s, so the glowing region lies along the path and fades as the vapour burns out. With the prop stationary, the same vapour rises into a teardrop. Heskestad's correlation L = 0.235 Q^(2/5) - 1.02 D gives about 0.3 m for a 5 cm wick at about 2.5 kW (derived: roughly 25 mL of kerosene over the guide's community figure of about 5 min burn). The flame puffs at f of about 1.5/sqrt(D), which is 5-7 Hz (Cetegen & Ahmed 1993 D^-1/2 scaling; the same fit gives about 15 Hz for a 1 cm candle). WHY IT BREAKS TODAY: C:/Humanity/src/renderer/particles.rs:330-335 and C:/Humanity/assets/shaders/particle_sim.wgsl:108 spawn a frame's particles at the emitter's end-of-frame position. At 10 m/s and 60 fps that is a clump every 16.7 cm, 2-3 flame widths apart, and even 144 Hz leaves 7 cm steps. TECHNIQUE: Lagrangian flame parcels. (a) Store each wick's previous and current world position (or angular velocity, for an exact arc). Spread each frame's emission along that sub-frame path and pre-age every parcel by its sub-frame offset. This alone removes the beads. (b) Each parcel carries temperature and soot mass. Velocity relaxes toward the local air velocity (drag, instead of the constant gravity at particles.rs:250-258), plus buoyancy proportional to (T-Ta)/Ta. Add curl-noise turbulence (Bridson, Hourihan and Nordenstam, SIGGRAPH 2007) sampled from a small precomputed 3D noise; the cloud noise machinery exists. Burnout time shortens as relative air speed rises (calibrate). (c) Shade from temperature. A blackbody lookup table built by integrating Planck against the CIE 1931 colour-matching functions into linear sRGB (Nguyen, Fedkiw and Jensen, SIGGRAPH 2002; Pegoraro and Parker, EG Natural Phenomena 2006, which adds per-fuel spectra and soot) replaces the linear colour_start to colour_end fade. Soot must absorb as well as emit, so flames need a premultiplied blend (emission + dst x transmittance) beside the pure alpha and additive states at particles.rs:626-647. Add a thin blue CH* 431 nm / C2* 516 nm band where vapour first meets air at the wick. Fuel choice (soot, colour, burn time) comes from data rows, never code. (d) Floating origin: world-anchored parcels need the GPU pool to take a rebase shift. The CPU path has one (particles.rs:476-487); the GPU pool does not. COST: one increment. It needs a trail emitter mode with a per-emitter parameter array (the GPU sim has one SimParams, particle_sim.wgsl:29-45), a flame fragment path and the blackbody table. 50 props at about 300 parcels is about 15k particles, trivial against the 4.19M-slot ceiling (particles_gpu.rs:22-24). ACCEPTANCE, new vantage firestaff-night-4m (22:00, grass, staff spinning 2 rev/s square to the camera, kerosene). EXPECT: "Each wick trails a continuous tapering tongue of flame roughly a quarter turn of arc (0.3-1 m) behind it: near-white-yellow at the wick, deepening through orange to a dull red thin tail, with a faint blue edge at the wick itself; nowhere near a full circle." REGRESSIONS: "no string-of-beads: the trail must not break into blobs spaced one frame of travel apart (end-of-frame spawn clumping)"; "no full-circle rings of fire (that is a long-exposure photograph, not what the eye sees)"; "no flame standing upright above a wick moving at speed (flame emitted in prop-local space)". Static companion firestaff-static-1m (spin 0). EXPECT: "one upright teardrop flame about 25-35 cm tall that visibly flickers several times a second". Measured gate: a 64-frame luminance series of the flame has its spectral peak between 3.5 and 10 Hz for a 5 cm wick.

#2 THE FLAME'S OWN LIGHT, MOVING, WARM, FLICKERING, CASTING THE PERFORMER'S SHADOW (1-50 m; the main cue beyond about 10 m; small cost for the lights, medium for shadows). MISSING CUE: from mid range a fire performer is read mostly from the warm pool of light sweeping over the ground and body, and the shadow swinging opposite the prop. A flame with no light, or a steady light, reads as a sticker. REAL BEHAVIOUR: a sooty flame's colour temperature is about 1850-1950 K (candle measurements run 1847-2626 K, 1914 K at the brightest point). A candle releases about 77 +/- 9 W of heat for about 12.6 lm (0.1-0.17 lm/W). Scaled to a roughly 2.5 kW wick, that is about 250-400 lm, like a 25-40 W incandescent bulb (derived estimate: verify with a lux meter at 1 m from a lit wick before putting it in data). Brightness flickers at the puffing frequency, and the source sweeps at about 10 m/s. TECHNIQUE: one light per wick, packed as the existing capsule LINE light (C:/Humanity/src/renderer/light.rs:104-113) from last frame's wick position to this frame's. The ground then shows the frame's swept emission as a smear instead of a point jumping 15 cm per frame. Intensity comes in lumens from the fuel row, colour from the same blackbody table. Luminance follows the parcel system's summed emission, so flicker is caused by the flame, not a separate random number. Forward+ already bins 2048 lights (C:/Humanity/src/renderer/light_tiles.rs:1-21), so dozens of props are affordable. SHADOWS: local lights cast none today. The 2030 answer is ReSTIR direct lighting (Bitterli et al., SIGGRAPH 2020) with ray-query shadow rays. wgpu exposes EXPERIMENTAL_RAY_QUERY: full on Vulkan, passthrough on DX12 and Metal, flagged as liable to breaking changes; the repo is on wgpu 24 (C:/Humanity/Cargo.toml:33). A rung that belongs to that architecture: screen-space contact shadows toward the 1-2 nearest flame lights (Bend Studio's Apache-2.0 code), plus one low-resolution cube shadow for the nearest performer. ACCEPTANCE, new vantage firepoi-night-10m (a performer with two poi, 22:00). EXPECT: "A warm orange pool lights the ground and the performer, visibly brighter on the side the poi are currently on, and the performer's shadow swings away from the flames." REGRESSIONS: "no light pool that stays centred on the performer while the flames swing (light parented to the body)"; "no neutral or white flame light (must read about 1900 K warm)"; "no steady unflickering flame light". Measured: ground-pixel chromaticity under the pool sits at 1700-2100 K CCT.

#3 A 16-BIT LINEAR HDR BUFFER BEFORE ANY FLAME CAN READ AS LIGHT (all ranges at night; decisive past about 20 m, where the flame is a few pixels and its glare IS its size; large cost, already planned). MISSING CUE: no near-white bleached core with a coloured falloff and a glare halo, and two overlapping flames are no brighter than one. REAL BEHAVIOUR: a flame's luminance is thousands of cd/m^2 (derived: a candle is about 1 cd from about 2.5 cm^2 of projected area, about 4000 cd/m^2) against a night scene at 10^-3 to 1 cd/m^2. Eye and camera both saturate the core toward white and spread veiling glare around it. WHY IT BREAKS TODAY: the scene target is the 8-bit sRGB swapchain format (C:/Humanity/src/renderer/surface.rs:171-194; C:/Humanity/src/renderer/mod.rs:1159-1165). Every PBR material tone-maps itself (C:/Humanity/assets/shaders/pbr/80-fragment-shared.wgsl:436-442). The particle shader writes rgb*(1+emissive) with no tone map into that 8-bit target (C:/Humanity/assets/shaders/particles.wgsl:92-94), so the fire, sparks, explosion and welding emissive values of 3-10 (C:/Humanity/data/particles.ron:23, 57, 195, 229) clip. Bloom exists but is never called (mod.rs:2045; C:/Humanity/src/gui/pages/performance.rs:526-534). TECHNIQUE: an Rgba16Float scene-referred target, one tone map after every layer, and bloom as energy-conserving glare. Use a multi-mip bloom like Jimenez's 'Next Generation Post Processing in Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare' (SIGGRAPH 2014), not a threshold. This is W5 of C:/Humanity/docs/design/environment-program.md:807, which says layers cannot be converted piecemeal. Fire work is gated on it: either pull that increment forward or accept that fire is judged on shape only until it lands. ACCEPTANCE (firestaff-night-4m and firepoi-night-10m). EXPECT: "Flame cores render near-white-yellow with a smooth orange-to-red falloff and a soft glow halo that widens with brightness; where two flames cross, the overlap is visibly brighter." REGRESSIONS: "no hard-edged flat clipped-yellow flame discs"; "no glow halo around non-emissive surfaces (bloom threshold or energy leak)".

#4 THE SPINNING PROP BODY NEEDS MOTION BLUR FOR ONE FRAME'S EXPOSURE, NOT A LONG EXPOSURE (1-20 m; medium-large cost for a velocity buffer, small for an exact analytic rung). MISSING CUE: a staff at 2 rev/s is drawn as a crisp stick jumping between poses. The eye sees a translucent blurred disc with a solid grip at the hub. REAL BEHAVIOUR: the tip moves about 9 m/s, which is about 15 cm per 60 Hz frame. The eye sums light over roughly 50-100 ms (Bloch's-law critical duration). A camera sums over its shutter; long-exposure photos (1/2 s and up) show the full circles people associate with fire poi. Displays add judder until about 250 fps (Kuroki et al., JSID 2007), and phantom-array doubling appears during eye movement across moving sampled lights. THE PHYSICALLY RIGHT TARGET: render what a camera with shutter about equal to the frame time sees, plus the real vapour trail (#1). Do NOT add retinal persistence on top, because the viewer's own eye integrates the screen. The one caveat: a display is far dimmer than a real flame, so the retina's own trail is shorter than in life. Restoring it is a taste call for the operator. TECHNIQUE: a per-object velocity buffer plus a reconstruction filter (McGuire, Hennessy, Bukowski and Osman, I3D 2012; Jimenez 2014). The engine has no motion vectors, TAA or motion blur (none found in C:/Humanity/src). A cheap rung that is exact for rigid rotation: draw the spinning prop as K sub-frame instances (K = angular travel / about 5 degrees) at 1/K weight. ACCEPTANCE (firestaff-night-4m). EXPECT: "The spinning shaft reads as a translucent blurred disc with the grip solid at its centre and the flames at its rim." REGRESSIONS: "no crisp multiple copies of the shaft (too few sub-frame instances)"; "no smear on the static background while the camera is still".

#5 SMOKE AMOUNT AND COLOUR FROM THE FUEL; SMOKE THAT FADES INTO GEOMETRY AND IS LIT FROM WITHIN (0.5-20 m; small cost for depth fade and fuel data, medium for six-way or froxel lighting). MISSING CUE: every fire gets the same grey puffs (C:/Humanity/data/particles.ron:26-42) with hard edges where sprites meet the ground or body. Real smoke colour and quantity follow the fuel, and near a flame the smoke is lit from inside and below. REAL BEHAVIOUR: flame smoke's specific extinction is about 8.7 m^2/g at 633 nm (Mulholland and Croarkin, Fire and Materials 2000). Fresh soot is strongly absorbing, with a mass absorption cross-section of 7.5 +/- 1.2 m^2/g at 550 nm (Bond and Bergstrom 2006), so it is black-brown, not grey. The repo's own guide: kerosene soots heavily, camp fuel is cleaner and bluer, alcohol hardly soots and is hard to see (C:/Humanity/docs/user/making/fire_staff_materials.md:117-123). Derived estimate: a 2.5 kW kerosene wick at a few-percent soot yield sheds a few mg/s. That gives optical depth of about 0.1-0.3 across the tail within about 0.5 m, diluting out within about 1 m (verify). White smoke is condensed water or fuel/wax vapour, for example after dousing a wick or the relightable white smoke of a snuffed candle. TECHNIQUE: smoke parcels continue from the flame parcels, inheriting soot mass as T drops. Extinction = soot mass x 8.7 m^2/g, with low albedo for fresh soot. Soft particles fade by scene depth (Lorach, NVIDIA 2007); the depth texture already allows sampling (C:/Humanity/src/renderer/surface.rs:211-212). Lighting: six-way lightmaps for baked puffs (Unity, 'Realistic smoke lighting with 6-way lighting', 2023; EmberGen exports these), or froxel injection (Hillaire, 'Physically Based and Unified Volumetric Rendering in Frostbite', SIGGRAPH 2015) for volumetric smoke with shadows. Real embers are carried by the plume, and they dim red-ward and vanish as they cool. REAL BEHAVIOUR: small particles reach terminal velocity within milliseconds and ride the updraft. Incandescent colour is blackbody, first dull red near 800 K. Radiated brightness falls with T^4, so cooling embers darken quickly. High-carbon steel sparks burst into branching stars, which is metallurgical spark testing and a genuine teaching cue. Real fire-prop specific: an overloaded wick flings burning fuel droplets off on a tangent, the reason spinners do a 'fuel dump' before lighting. TECHNIQUE: per-particle temperature and mass; quadratic drag toward the shared air-velocity field; emission from the same blackbody table with Stefan-Boltzmann scaling; an optional data-driven burst event for steel. #8 HEAT HAZE (0.5-10 m; small-medium cost; physically subtle for props, larger for campfires and explosions). MISSING CUE: background edges above and behind the flame do not shimmer. REAL BEHAVIOUR: by the Gladstone-Dale relation (refractivity proportional to air density), air at 600 K has about half the refractivity of ambient air. Derived estimate: a 5-10 cm prop plume bends rays by about 10^-3 rad, roughly one pixel at 1080p with a 60 degree field of view. A campfire plume bends them by several pixels. The shimmer shows only against textured backgrounds, grows with the background's distance from the plume, and is invisible against open sky (schlieren principle; Settles, 'Schlieren and Shadowgraph Techniques', 2001). TECHNIQUE: copy scene colour before the transparent draw, then have distortion sprites riding the hot parcels offset the UVs by a curl-noise normal scaled by temperature (Sousa, 'Generic Refraction Simulation', GPU Gems 2 ch. 19, 2005). ACCEPTANCE (firestaff-static-dusk-1m, with a fence or wall behind). EXPECT: "Straight edges seen just above the flame wobble by about a pixel, flickering with the flame." REGRESSIONS: "no shimmer against open sky"; "no whole-screen wobble"; "no distortion applied to the flame's own pixels in front of the plume".

#9 THE EMBERGEN-CLASS TIERS: A LIVE GRID SIMULATION FOR THE NEAREST FLAMES, AND BAKED VOLUMES FOR ONE-OFF EFFECTS (large cost). MISSING CUE: particle flames lack the vortex shedding, curling and tearing that a real fluid produces; explosions need rolling, self-shadowed fireballs. REAL BEHAVIOUR: puffing is a buoyant instability in which a ring-shaped vortex forms just above the fuel (Cetegen and Ahmed 1993). TECHNIQUE, TIER B (within about 10 m, the 1-4 nearest sources): a GPU combustion simulation on a grid anchored in the world around the performer that stores only occupied cells. NVIDIA Flow 2.2 is the open reference (real-time sparse-voxel fluid simulation 'that includes a combustion model'; HLSL compute; BSD-3 since PhysX 5.6, April 2025), so it can be ported to WGSL rather than reinvented. Foundations: Stam's 'Stable Fluids' (1999); Fedkiw, Stam and Jensen's vorticity confinement (2001); Kim et al.'s wavelet turbulence for extra detail (2008); Crane, Llamas and Tariq, GPU Gems 3 ch. 30 (fire and smoke on the GPU). Its airflow moves the Tier A parcels, and its temperature and soot grids can be ray-marched with the Nubis cloud machinery (commit 1f9faa40). Derived cost estimate: about 1 ms per 64^3 domain at 3 cm cells on the RTX 4070, to be measured with the rig. TIER C (authored one-shots at any distance): run the same solver offline, then bake either animated texture sheets with motion vectors (Klemen Lozar's frame blending, a variation of Guerrilla's Killzone 2 technique) plus emissive and six-way lighting maps, or sparse volume sequences (OpenVDB, or NanoVDB for the GPU). Unreal Engine 5.3's Sparse Volume Textures, which import VDB sequences, are the industry precedent. ACCEPTANCE (hero close-up of a static staff or campfire). EXPECT: "The flame surface tears into curling tongues that roll upward and pinch off in pulses several times a second." REGRESSIONS: "no visible voxel stair-steps or box edge where the simulation domain ends"; "no loop seam or pop in a baked sheet or volume".

#10 ASTEROID IMPACT, DRIVEN BY REAL IMPACT PHYSICS (secondary; large cost; ranges from 100 m to orbit). MISSING CUE: nothing renders (vfx_asteroid is unused, C:/Humanity/src/systems/disasters.rs:105). REAL CUES IN ORDER: (1) Entry: a bolide brighter than the Sun and a persistent dust trail lit by sunlight and twisted by winds. At Chelyabinsk the shock wave reached Korkino 87.5 s after peak brightness, so at distance the flash always precedes the boom by distance/343 m/s. (2) Contact: a vapour plume fireball that rises and expands. Beyond the curvature horizon it cannot be seen (Collins, Melosh and Marcus 2005). (3) Air blast: a hemispherical shock whose passage lifts a skirt of dust and, in humid air, a brief condensation shell. (4) Ejecta curtain: an inverted cone thrown out at about 45 degrees that sweeps outward across the ground. Material from farther out launches later and slower and lands nearer the rim. Ejecta blanket thickness falls roughly as distance^-3 (McGetchin et al. 1973, used by Collins et al.), with rays and secondary craters. Oblique impacts throw lopsided ejecta. In space, DART's plume on Dimorphos was a cone with a 140 +/- 4 degree opening, full of filaments and boulders, blue near the asteroid and redder farther out (LICIACube, Nature 2024). (5) Crater: a bowl that forms and then partly collapses. Small impacts leave simple bowls; larger ones leave complex craters with central peaks and terraces. (6) Aftermath: a rising dust column, and fires started by the heat pulse near the site. TECHNIQUE: compute sizes and timings from the Earth Impact Effects Program equations (inputs are diameter, density, velocity, angle, target type and distance), with baked Tier C volumes for the fireball and plume, GPU particle ejecta for the curtain, and terrain deformation for the crater. ACCEPTANCE, new vantage impact-300m-20km (a 300 m stony impactor at 20 km/s, viewer 20 km away). EXPECT: "A flash lights the horizon first; a rising fireball and an inverted-cone curtain of ejecta spread from the site; the air-blast dust skirt and the sound arrive about a minute later (20 km / 343 m/s = 58 s)." REGRESSIONS: "no simultaneous flash and boom at distance"; "no spherical particle burst instead of an inverted-cone ejecta curtain"; "crater and fireball sizes must match the Earth Impact Effects Program for the same inputs within 20 percent".

WHAT EMBERGEN ACTUALLY IS (JangaFX, checked 2026-09-24): an authoring tool whose GPU solver runs in real time for the artist while designing, then exports image sequences and flipbooks (EXR/PNG/TGA) with channels including final render, motion vectors, 6-point lighting, normals and depth, plus VDB volumes. The product page says nothing about a runtime or SDK for running the simulation inside a shipped game, so it is a bake tool. A search snippet attributes to JangaFX the claim that 'a 6 GiB GPU can simulate up to 200 million active (sparse) voxels'; the page was not reachable (HTTP 401), so treat that as unverified. Licensing EmberGen as an authoring tool would be the operator's decision. The repo rule is to use public techniques, never proprietary code or assets. NVIDIA Flow (BSD-3) is the open solver to learn from or port.

MMO FEASIBILITY, dozens of props: Tier A (flame parcels, one light each) scales to every visible prop. Tier B (live grid simulation) is affordable only for the 1-4 nearest sources. Tier C (baked volumes and sheets) costs nothing to simulate at run time and is for authored one-shots. A single shared, low-resolution air-velocity field around the camera that every flame, smoke plume and ember reads is what makes a gust bend all of them together (the motion-coherence cue). It serves weather, leaves and dust as well.

EYE VERSUS CAMERA, the subtle point behind #1 and #4: photos of fire poi usually show full circles because of long exposures; the naked eye sees roughly 0.3-1 m arcs, which is the physical vapour trail plus the retina's roughly 50-100 ms integration. The game should draw the physical trail plus one frame's motion blur and let the viewer's eye add its own persistence. Whether to add a short extra 'retinal' trail, to make up for a display being far dimmer than a real flame, is a TASTE CALL for the operator, not a physics answer.

GASES YOU CANNOT SEE: combustion makes CO2, water vapour and CO, all invisible. Realism says do not draw them. Visible products are soot (black), and condensed water or fuel/wax aerosol (white, for example when dousing a wick). For the education and MMO depth the operator wants, an optional analysis view (a thermal-camera look or a gas-concentration overlay from the same parcel data) teaches without faking the normal view. That is a design/taste call for the operator. Coloured-fire additives used in fire performance emit narrow spectral lines, not a blackbody curve, so if supported they need a per-additive line-colour term from data, never a tint.
SODIUM CUE: dust, sweat or salt on a wick adds the 589 nm sodium line and pushes the flame more orange. It is a small but true cue; the same line-colour term covers it.

DERIVED NUMBERS TO MEASURE BEFORE THEY BECOME DATA: wick heat release about 2.5 kW (from an assumed 25 mL soak and the guide's community burn times); light output 250-400 lm; prop speed 9-13 m/s; flame tail 0.3-1 m; smoke optical depth 0.1-0.3; heat-haze deflection about 10^-3 rad; Tier B cost about 1 ms per 64^3 domain. Each can be calibrated from a 240 fps phone video of a real staff (count frames for trail length and flicker) plus a lux meter reading at 1 m.

SOUND belongs to the audio lane, not rendering. The fire-prop 'whoosh' is turbulent combustion noise that rises with speed, and the impact's delayed boom is covered in #10. Both are strong realism cues worth a separate audio pass.
